````text
# Copy to .env and fill in. Never commit .env.
# Generate the three secrets at the bottom with:  npm run keygen

# --- Database (Neon or any Postgres) -----------------------------------
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@host/db?sslmode=require

# --- LLM (Gemini free tier) --------------------------------------------
LLM_PROVIDER=gemini
GEMINI_API_KEY=
GEMINI_MODEL=gemini-3.5-flash-lite
GEMINI_FALLBACK_MODEL=gemini-3.1-flash-lite
GEMINI_LAST_RESORT_MODEL=gemma-4-31b-it
GEMINI_RPD_LIMIT=500

# --- LinkedIn app ------------------------------------------------------
# From https://www.linkedin.com/developers/apps -> Auth tab.
LINKEDIN_CLIENT_ID=
LINKEDIN_CLIENT_SECRET=
# Must match a redirect URL registered on the app EXACTLY, byte for byte.
LINKEDIN_REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost:3000/api/linkedin/callback
# Versioned APIs expire about a year out; bump this rather than editing code.
LINKEDIN_API_VERSION=202607

# THE SAFETY SWITCH. While this is anything but "true", the agent drafts and
# queues normally but nothing is ever sent to LinkedIn. Leave it off until
# you have read a few drafts and like them.
LINKEDIN_LIVE=false

# --- ByLine native client (service-owned settings, never entered by clients) ---
BYLINE_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:3000
GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=
GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=
GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost:3000/api/native-auth/callback
BYLINE_AI_CALLS_PER_USER_DAY=60
# Enable on a hosted release after running npm run migrate against its database.
BYLINE_REQUIRE_MIGRATIONS=false
# Local fixture mode requires BOTH flags. Keep both false in hosted environments.
BYLINE_TEST_MODE=false
BYLINE_LOCAL_ONLY=false

# Backstop against a logic error looping the publisher. LinkedIn's own member
# limit is 150 requests/day; this is deliberately far below it.
DAILY_POST_CAP=3

# --- Secrets (npm run keygen) ------------------------------------------
# Encrypts LinkedIn tokens at rest. Rotating it invalidates stored tokens and
# requires reconnecting — which is the intended behaviour, not a bug.
TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY=
# Signs the dashboard session cookie.
APP_SECRET=
# The dashboard password. Anyone with this can publish as you.
APP_PASSWORD=
# Header value the cron endpoint requires.
CRON_SECRET=

# --- Optional: Breeth graph memory -------------------------------------
# Omit entirely and the agent falls back to Postgres fingerprints.
BREETH_API_KEY=

# ---- Push notifications (optional, free)
# From the Firebase console: Project settings -> Service accounts ->
# "Generate new private key". The JSON it downloads has all three of these.
# Leave them unset and the app behaves exactly as before, minus notifications.
# FCM_PRIVATE_KEY keeps its \n escapes — do not paste real newlines.
FCM_PROJECT_ID=
FCM_CLIENT_EMAIL=
FCM_PRIVATE_KEY=

````

## Source: .github/workflows/backup.yml

````text
# A nightly encrypted dump of the database, kept as a build artifact.
#
# The parts that cannot be recreated are the published archive, the writing
# samples and the edit notes — the agent's whole learned voice. Everything else
# in the app can be rebuilt from code; those cannot be rebuilt from anything.
#
# Encrypted BEFORE it leaves the runner, with a passphrase this workflow never
# prints. The dump contains the LinkedIn token, and although that column is
# already encrypted with TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY (which is NOT in the dump), an
# artifact is still not the place for a bare copy of the database.
#
# Free: private repos get 2,000 Actions minutes and 500 MB of artifact storage
# a month. A dump of this app is a few megabytes and this job takes about a
# minute, so a full 90-day history stays comfortably inside the free tier.
name: Backup

on:
  schedule:
    # 19:40 UTC — a quiet hour for Asia/Kolkata, and deliberately not on the
    # hour, when GitHub's scheduler is most congested and most likely to delay.
    - cron: "40 19 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  dump:
    name: encrypted pg_dump
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Check the secrets are present
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
          BACKUP_PASSPHRASE: ${{ secrets.BACKUP_PASSPHRASE }}
        run: |
          test -n "$DATABASE_URL" || { echo "::error::DATABASE_URL secret is not set"; exit 1; }
          test -n "$BACKUP_PASSPHRASE" || { echo "::error::BACKUP_PASSPHRASE secret is not set"; exit 1; }

      - name: Dump and encrypt
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
          BACKUP_PASSPHRASE: ${{ secrets.BACKUP_PASSPHRASE }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          stamp="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)"

          # pg_dump runs inside a pinned postgres image rather than using the
          # runner's client. A pg_dump OLDER than the server refuses to run, and
          # the runner's version is whatever Ubuntu ships this month — which is
          # a build that breaks by itself the day the database is upgraded.
          # Newer-client-than-server is the supported direction, so this tracks
          # the newest release rather than the one the database happens to be on.
          # -alpine: the same pg_dump from a ~100MB image instead of ~450MB.
          # The pull is the entire cost of this job — the dump itself takes a
          # second — and a runner starts with an empty image cache every time,
          # so the image size is very nearly the whole wall clock.
          docker run --rm postgres:18-alpine \
            pg_dump --no-owner --no-privileges --format=custom "$DATABASE_URL" \
            > "backup-$stamp.dump"

          test -s "backup-$stamp.dump" || { echo "::error::the dump is empty"; exit 1; }

          ls -lh "backup-$stamp.dump"

          # Symmetric AES-256. --batch and --passphrase-fd keep the passphrase
          # off the process list, where every other process on the box can read it.
          printf '%s' "$BACKUP_PASSPHRASE" | gpg --batch --yes --symmetric \
            --cipher-algo AES256 --passphrase-fd 0 \
            --output "backup-$stamp.dump.gpg" "backup-$stamp.dump"

          # The plaintext must not survive to the upload step.
          shred -u "backup-$stamp.dump" 2>/dev/null || rm -f "backup-$stamp.dump"
          echo "STAMP=$stamp" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Upload
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: db-backup-${{ env.STAMP }}
          path: backup-${{ env.STAMP }}.dump.gpg
          # The maximum GitHub allows, and the maximum the free tier costs
          # nothing for at this size.
          retention-days: 90
          if-no-files-found: error

````

## Source: .github/workflows/ci-mobile.yml

````text
# The Flutter checks, split out of ci.yml so they only run when the app changes.
#
# This is the expensive job — it provisions a Flutter toolchain and takes around
# three minutes, against roughly one for the backend jobs. Running it on every
# backend commit was paying for a toolchain the change could not possibly have
# affected.
#
# The minutes are not free here. A private repo on the GitHub free plan gets
# 2,000 Actions minutes a month and every job is rounded UP to a whole minute.
# Exhausting them does not degrade gracefully: Actions stop entirely until the
# next billing cycle, which silently takes the nightly backup and the watchdog
# with them — the two things that exist to notice failure.
name: CI (mobile)

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "mobile/**"
      - ".github/workflows/ci-mobile.yml"
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "mobile/**"
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: ci-mobile-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  mobile:
    name: flutter analyze and test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: mobile
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with:
          channel: stable
          # Caches the SDK between runs. Without it this job spends most of its
          # time downloading a toolchain that has not changed.
          cache: true
      - run: flutter pub get
      - name: Analyze
        run: flutter analyze lib test
      - name: Widget and transport tests
        run: flutter test

````

## Source: .github/workflows/ci.yml

````text
# Runs the checks that used to run only when someone remembered.
#
# The database job is the point of this file. scripts/selftest.ts is pure logic
# and never opens a connection, so invalid SQL that is valid TypeScript passed
# every check — which is how the scheduler shipped completely broken. The
# `database` job below runs every query against a real Postgres.
#
# Free on this repo: GitHub gives private repos 2,000 Actions minutes a month
# and this whole file is a few minutes per push.
name: CI

# Split from the Flutter checks so a backend change does not pay for a Flutter
# toolchain it did not touch, and a documentation change pays for nothing. See
# the note in ci-mobile.yml about why the minutes matter.
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore:
      - "mobile/**"
      - "**.md"
      - ".github/workflows/watchdog.yml"
      - ".github/workflows/backup.yml"
  pull_request:
  # So it can be run by hand after changing a secret, without an empty commit.
  workflow_dispatch:

# A newer push to the same branch makes an in-flight run pointless.
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  backend:
    name: types, logic, build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          # Matches the Vercel runtime. A CI on an older major can pass while
          # production breaks on a behaviour that changed between them, which is
          # the one thing a CI must never do.
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Typecheck
        run: npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json
      - name: Logic tests
        run: npm test
      - name: Production build
        # Builds into .next-verify so it can never clobber a real .next.
        run: npm run build:check

  database:
    name: real SQL against real Postgres
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    # A throwaway Postgres for this job only. Nothing here touches the live
    # database, and it is destroyed with the runner.
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
          POSTGRES_DB: linkdin_dbtest
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
        ports:
          - 5432:5432

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Integration tests
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/linkdin_dbtest
        run: npm run test:db



````

## Source: .github/workflows/watchdog.yml

````text
# The outside observer.
#
# This exists because of one structural fact: a dead scheduler cannot report its
# own death. If the cron tick is what checks whether ticks are happening, then
# the single failure that most needs an alert produces silence instead.
#
# So this runs on GitHub's infrastructure, on a different schedule, hitting
# /api/watchdog — which checks the scheduler heartbeat and the LinkedIn token
# and pushes to the phone if either has gone bad. The two can only fail
# together if GitHub and the app host are both down, which is a different and
# much louder kind of day.
#
# GitHub's cron is unreliable — it floors at 5 minutes and often runs 15+ late.
# That is fine HERE and would not be fine for the tick: this is asking "has
# anything been wrong for a while", not "is anything due right now".
#
# EVERY THREE HOURS, and the reason is billing rather than taste. A private repo
# on the free plan gets 2,000 Actions minutes a month, and every job is rounded
# UP to a whole minute — so this fifteen-second curl costs one minute a run.
# Every thirty minutes was 48 runs a day, 1,440 minutes a month, 72% of the
# entire allowance spent watching. Running out does not degrade anything
# gracefully: Actions stop dead until the next cycle, taking the backups and
# this watchdog with them, which is the exact outage it exists to report.
#
# Eight runs a day costs 240 minutes and detects a dead scheduler within three
# hours. The agent posts a few times a day, so the worst case is noticing one
# missed slot late — against a monitor that stops working every month.
name: Watchdog

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 */3 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      deep:
        description: "Verify the push credentials really mint a token (sends nothing)"
        type: boolean
        default: false
      test:
        description: "Send a real test notification to every registered phone"
        type: boolean
        default: false

jobs:
  check:
    name: is anything wrong
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Ask the app how it is
        env:
          APP_URL: ${{ secrets.APP_URL }}
          CRON_SECRET: ${{ secrets.CRON_SECRET }}
        run: |
          set -uo pipefail
          test -n "$APP_URL" || { echo "::error::APP_URL secret is not set"; exit 1; }
          test -n "$CRON_SECRET" || { echo "::error::CRON_SECRET secret is not set"; exit 1; }

          # --max-time so a hung host fails the step instead of holding a runner
          # for six hours. Retries because a cold start on a free tier can take
          # ten seconds and a single timeout is not news.
          # The scheduled run never asks for the deep check: it answers "is the
          # scheduler alive" and has no business calling Google to do it.
          path="/api/watchdog"
          if [ "${{ inputs.deep }}" = "true" ]; then path="$path?deep=1"; fi
          if [ "${{ inputs.test }}" = "true" ]; then path="$path?test=1"; fi

          body="$(curl -sS --max-time 45 --retry 3 --retry-delay 10 --retry-all-errors \
            -H "X-Cron-Secret: $CRON_SECRET" \
            -w '\n%{http_code}' \
            "$APP_URL$path")" || {
              echo "::error::could not reach $APP_URL — the app itself may be down"
              exit 1
            }

          code="$(printf '%s' "$body" | tail -n1)"
          json="$(printf '%s' "$body" | sed '$d')"
          echo "$json"

          if [ "$code" = "404" ]; then
            echo "::error::404 — CRON_SECRET does not match the deployed one"
            exit 1
          fi
          test "$code" = "200" || { echo "::error::watchdog returned HTTP $code"; exit 1; }

          # Surfaced in the Actions run as well as pushed to the phone, so the
          # history of "when did this start" is readable without a database.
          # Two shapes. The deep check reports credentials; the normal run
          # reports alerts. Neither may be mistaken for the other.
          if printf %s "$json" | grep -qF '"test":true'; then
            printf %s "$json" | grep -qF '"ok":true'               && echo "test notification sent - check the phone"               || { echo "::error::the test notification was not delivered - see the JSON above"; exit 1; }
          elif printf %s "$json" | grep -qF '"deep":true'; then
            printf %s "$json" | grep -qF '"ok":true' \
              && echo "push credentials verified" \
              || { echo "::error::push credentials are NOT working - see the JSON above"; exit 1; }
          elif printf %s "$json" | grep -qF '"alerts":[]'; then
            echo "healthy"
          else
            echo "::warning::the watchdog raised alerts - see the JSON above"
          fi

````

## Source: BYLINE-LIVE.md

````text
# ByLine with real services and a zero budget

This development environment uses the existing Gemini and LinkedIn application credentials on your computer. Google’s billing API was checked before generation: billing was disabled for the Gemini project and Firebase project. Nothing enables billing, buys credits, or provisions a paid host.

## Start

```powershell
npm run local:setup
npm run live:setup
npm run live:dev
```

The live launcher serves localhost:3000 and runs the scheduler every 30 seconds. It uses a separate local database, `byline_live`. The original `.env`, hosted database and original phone application are preserved. The demo remains on port 3100 with database `byline_local`.

The Firebase CLI must already be signed into the project. The launcher refreshes a short-lived operator access token for FCM; no service-account private key is required for local testing. That token stays in an ignored local file. This operator login is a development credential source, not a credential to distribute to customers or embed in an APK.

The launcher periodically checks the Gemini project’s billing status. AI requests require a recent successful verification tied to the configured API key; expired, missing or mismatched verification blocks generation. Free-tier quota exhaustion is handled as an unavailable writer, not a paid upgrade. Never turn on billing for this environment.

## Android

```powershell
./scripts/build-live-android.ps1
./scripts/install-live-android.ps1
```

Open **ByLine Live** (`com.linkdin.byline`), choose **Continue with LinkedIn**, complete your own sign-in and consent, then use **Return to ByLine**. Complete topics, voice, sample acceptance, delivery time and notifications. There is no client API-key form or company/developer-app setup.

After setup, **Prepare today’s post** runs the real source-discovery, scoring and writing pipeline immediately. It reuses the current day’s suggestion if one already exists. Read the post and source first. **Approve publishes to your connected LinkedIn profile for real.** Edit and Skip remain available. Nothing in the smoke tests presses Approve or publishes a test post.

Use **Settings → Daily delivery → Send a test notification** to verify FCM on the handset. Test with the app in the background too. Keep the USB cable connected; the installer forwards localhost:3000 from the phone to the computer. After reconnecting, run `adb reverse tcp:3000 tcp:3000` again. The server and computer must remain awake for generation and delivery.

Google sign-in is implemented but its service-owned OAuth client is not configured in the current installation. LinkedIn is the configured sign-in route. Signing in through a different provider currently creates a separate account; provider linking remains release work.

### LinkedIn callback registration (app owner only)

For this USB-connected development build, the existing LinkedIn developer application must include `http://localhost:3000/api/linkedin/callback` under **Auth → OAuth 2.0 settings → Authorized redirect URLs**. Add this alongside existing URLs so the original installation keeps working. This must belong to the application whose client ID is configured in `.env.byline-live`; changing a different LinkedIn application will not fix sign-in.

The live server sends that exact callback, and the Android installer forwards port 3000 over USB. A LinkedIn error saying the redirect URL does not match the registered value requires correcting the registration before authorization can finish. After saving, cancel the pending sign-in in ByLine Live and start a new attempt. No APK rebuild is needed for the portal change. This is a one-time owner configuration, never a customer onboarding step.

## Windows

```powershell
cd mobile
flutter build windows --release --dart-define=BYLINE_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 --dart-define=BYLINE_APP_VARIANT=live
```

Run `mobile/build/windows/x64/runner/Release/ByLine.exe`, keeping the whole Release directory together. Sign in with the same LinkedIn account to use the same data as your phone. Native Windows notifications check for new drafts while ByLine is open or minimized; closing the application stops desktop checks. Android FCM is the background delivery route when the desktop application is closed.

## Light interface and flexible preferences

The Android and Windows clients now use a light slate-and-blue interface with dark readable text, softer surfaces, and responsive navigation. Desktop uses a navigation rail and bounded reading columns; phones retain labelled bottom navigation.

- **Voice:** type your own writing instructions and paste previous posts first. Presets are optional. Expand **Fine-tune your writing** for structure, opening/closing, audience, length, hashtags, signature and banned phrases. Save and Preview remain available.
- **Topics:** add/remove personal interests in your own words, then **Save interests**. Up to 12 interests are supported after onboarding. Source coverage remains independently selectable below, so changing interests preserves feed choices and writing style.
- **Daily delivery:** choose an exact time, including individual minutes, and edit the timezone. Quick choices are shortcuts. Advanced publishing slots and daily approval delivery are described separately.
- **Daily use:** read the draft and source, then Approve, Edit or Skip. Advanced draft controls, composer, attachments, rewrites, archive, connection and diagnostics remain available.

The research and implementation plan is in `reports/ByLine-UX-redesign-plan.md`. Widget-rendered previews using synthetic data are in `reports/ui-preview`; these are not screenshots of your private account.

Updated local artifacts: `.byline-local/byline-live.apk` (Android debug build for direct testing) and `.byline-local/ByLine-Windows.zip` (extract the entire archive before running `ByLine.exe`). Both still target localhost:3000. Updating Android with the install script preserves the existing ByLine Live session and data.

## Backup

```powershell
npm run live:backup
```

Backups are private PostgreSQL archives under `.byline-local/backups`. Keep the matching `.env.byline-live` encryption key with your private backup process; encrypted LinkedIn credentials cannot be recovered without it. Restore into a new database first and validate the result before replacing any working database.

## Verification and remaining handoffs

Real Gemini generation and the full discovery → scoring → writing pipeline were exercised successfully. No LinkedIn post was published by the automated pipeline tests. On 2026-09-06, the owner reported successful phone onboarding, voice setup, draft preparation and publishing to their LinkedIn profile. A separate background FCM test was then sent with the owner's confirmation: Google accepted delivery to one registered device, Android recorded the ByLine test notification, and a phone screenshot confirmed it in the notification shade. The Android foreground notification path was subsequently updated so messages also appear in the notification shade while ByLine is open. The rebuilt APK was installed, and the in-app test button was exercised on the handset: Android recorded the test notification and the shade showed it. The original banner remains a fallback when system notifications are disabled. Scheduled daily delivery still needs end-to-end handset verification.

This setup is functional local infrastructure, not free always-on hosting: it stops when the computer sleeps or the server stops. Public distribution still needs HTTPS hosting/callback configuration, release signing/update distribution, privacy/support material, account export/deletion, provider linking and any requested migration of original history. LinkedIn recent-post import is not implemented; pasted voice examples work without restricted history access.
````

## Source: BYLINE-LOCAL.md

````text
# ByLine: free local development and phone testing

The native ByLine client shares the existing publishing engine. The new local preview installs as `com.linkdin.byline_preview`, alongside the original application. It uses a separate PostgreSQL database and a backend on port 3100. The original `.env`, provider accounts, application ID and saved history are not replaced.

## Start the local system

For a connected Android phone on Windows, run `npm run local:phone`. This prepares
the isolated database, starts the backend in the background if needed, builds the
preview APK if missing, and installs and opens it over USB. Use
`npm run local:phone -- -Rebuild` after changing Flutter code. Server logs are in
`.byline-local/server.stdout.log` and `.byline-local/server.stderr.log`.

To run the backend in a visible terminal instead:

From the repository root:

```powershell
npm run local:setup
npm run local:dev
```

Keep the second terminal running. Setup uses PostgreSQL 18 already installed on this computer and creates `.byline-local/postgres` on localhost port 55440, plus ignored `.env.byline-local` secrets. It never reads or copies your Gemini, LinkedIn or Firebase credentials. Set `PG_BIN` to another PostgreSQL installation directory if needed.

The launcher binds the API to localhost and ticks the existing scheduler every 30 seconds. Sleeping or shutting down the computer stops it. Data survives restarts. This local database uses trust authentication on the loopback interface for development; do not expose its port to the network.

## Install on Android without a store

Enable USB debugging on your Android phone and connect the cable. Run:

```powershell
./scripts/build-local-android.ps1
./scripts/install-local-android.ps1
```

The installer forwards the phone's localhost:3100 to the computer over USB and opens ByLine. Re-run it, or `adb reverse tcp:3100 tcp:3100`, after reconnecting a phone if the app cannot reach the server. Keep the cable connected for this setup. No server address or API key is entered in normal onboarding.

On the welcome screen choose **Try local preview**, complete topics/voice/sample acceptance/time, then choose **Not now** for notifications. Use the preparation action on the home screen to create a demonstration draft for today's Timetable entry. Edit, skip, composer, archive and voice settings remain available. Each timetable entry produces at most one draft per local calendar day; repeated preparation does not replace an existing, skipped or published draft.

Local samples are explicitly labelled demonstrations. They exercise the app and database without calling Gemini. Local approvals move a post into the local archive and are labelled simulations; they never call LinkedIn. Notifications accurately report unavailable in this environment because the launcher clears Firebase credentials. Physical FCM delivery needs a separately configured integration run.

The local APK disables Google Services processing and uses a separate application ID; this is intentional. It does not impersonate the Firebase registration of your original app.

## Windows desktop

```powershell
cd mobile
flutter build windows --release --dart-define=BYLINE_API_URL=http://localhost:3100 --dart-define=BYLINE_LOCAL_TEST=true
```

Run `mobile/build/windows/x64/runner/Release/ByLine.exe` with the whole Release directory present. The first build downloads the Firebase C++ build dependency. The native Windows client uses the same account and API. Windows push delivery is not implemented by the Android Firebase Messaging plugin; the desktop application reports notifications unavailable. Review through the phone or open desktop app.

## Real integrations, when ready

The local launcher intentionally disables external credentials and publishing, even if the original `.env` contains them. To test real provider consent or real Gemini output, use a separately configured environment with test content appropriate for Gemini's free-service terms. Do not enable billing for local development.

- ByLine owns Google OAuth credentials (`GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`, optional `GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI`). The default callback is `/api/native-auth/callback` under `BYLINE_PUBLIC_URL`.
- LinkedIn uses the existing ByLine-owned developer app and `LINKEDIN_REDIRECT_URI`, normally `/api/linkedin/callback`. The callback supports both legacy connection and native sign-in. Customers need no company Page or developer app.
- Native sign-in uses the external system browser. A random verifier protects a single-use completion exchange; the app polls the authenticated flow and continues automatically. Cancelling or killing the app before completing sign-in may require restarting consent.
- Native session credentials are stored using the platform secure-storage plugin. Sessions have separate account identities and server-side revocation. Legacy password login remains under **Existing installation** for the original owner.
- Set the API URL at build time with `--dart-define=BYLINE_API_URL=https://your-backend`. A client web dashboard is not needed. An HTTPS callback and public privacy/support pages remain service infrastructure.
- Existing accounts are not silently assigned to a public signup. Moving existing history to a social-login account requires an explicit, verified owner migration; the old login continues to work meanwhile.

## Verification

```powershell
npm test
npx tsx scripts/byline-logic-test.ts
node scripts/byline-test.mjs
npm run test:local
npm run build:check
cd mobile
flutter analyze lib test
flutter test --no-pub
```

`test:local` requires the local launcher and runs the account/Timetable, catalogue API and native OAuth return suites. It creates isolated test accounts and checks ownership, activation, stale samples, asynchronous preparation, deduplication, simultaneous composer saves, simulated publishing and logout. It never uses the original database. The existing `test:db` suite must likewise run against a disposable/local database.

## Production boundary

Implemented capabilities include individual accounts, native OAuth completion, resumable saved onboarding, source-based Gemini previews, sample acceptance, separate daily review delivery, durable delivery retries and a notification outbox, application AI allowances, per-model shared pacing, token-usage records, source links, and local/desktop packaging.

This is a testable implementation, not a certification of public production readiness. Before admitting customers, validate actual provider grants and callback URLs, Gemini quota/data handling and measured costs, physical notification delivery, desktop notification strategy, release signing/update distribution, backup restoration, account export/deletion including optional external memory, and an explicit migration for existing history. Quiet days can still produce no post after retrying when no source clears the existing quality threshold. Exact push arrival time and automatic LinkedIn history import are not guaranteed.

Database changes are additive and recorded by schema hash in `byline_schema_versions`, under a transactional advisory lock. For a hosted deployment, first back up the selected database, configure that deployment's `DATABASE_URL`, and run `npm run migrate`. Set `BYLINE_REQUIRE_MIGRATIONS=true` in the serving environment so a release fails closed if its migration has not run. Existing installations keep automatic initialization by default for compatibility. The original hosted database has not been migrated as part of this local build.

No paid service is required or enabled by these local commands.

````

## Source: DEPLOY.md

````text
# Deploying

Everything here only runs while `npm run dev` is up on a laptop. Deploying is
what removes that — no dev server, no adb, no PowerShell tick loop.

Do these in order. Steps 1–4 are required for anything to work at all.

---

## 1. Import the repo into Vercel

New Project → import `link_agent` → framework auto-detects as Next.js.

**Do not deploy yet.** Set the environment variables first (step 2), or the
first build comes up with no database and no keys.

## 2. Environment variables

Copy every variable from your local `.env` into Project Settings →
Environment Variables, for **Production** and **Preview**.

Two must CHANGE rather than be copied:

| Variable | Local | Deployed |
|---|---|---|
| `LINKEDIN_REDIRECT_URI` | `http://localhost:3000/api/linkedin/callback` | `https://<your-app>.vercel.app/api/linkedin/callback` |
| `LINKEDIN_LIVE` | whatever you have | `true` when you want it posting for real |

Everything else — `DATABASE_URL`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, the model cascade,
`TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `APP_SECRET`, `APP_PASSWORD`, `CRON_SECRET` — copies
across unchanged.

`TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in particular must be **byte-identical** to the local
one, or every stored LinkedIn token becomes undecryptable and you will have to
reconnect.

## 3. Enable Fluid compute

Project Settings → Functions → **Fluid compute: on**.

Not optional. Without it a Hobby function is capped at **60 seconds**; with it,
300. A generation cycle takes 30–90 seconds per slot and they run serialized,
so on a 60-second cap the tick gets killed part-way and slots fail with no
clear reason. `vercel.json` asks for `maxDuration: 300`, which Vercel silently
lowers if Fluid compute is off.

## 4. Tell LinkedIn about the new redirect

LinkedIn Developer Portal → your app → Auth → **Authorized redirect URLs**, add:

```
https://<your-app>.vercel.app/api/linkedin/callback
```

Then open the deployed app, sign in, and **Reconnect** on the Status tab. The
existing token was issued against `localhost` and will not work.

## 5. Point a cron at the tick

Nothing generates or sends without this. `/api/cron/tick` is the only driver.

Use [cron-job.org](https://cron-job.org) — free, and every minute if you want:

- **URL** `https://<your-app>.vercel.app/api/cron/tick`
- **Every** 5 minutes
- **Header** `X-Cron-Secret: <your CRON_SECRET>`

Do **not** use Vercel's own cron on Hobby — it permits once per day. Do not use
GitHub Actions — it floors at 5 minutes and routinely runs 15+ minutes late,
which breaks the review-window promise.

The Schedule tab shows a red **SCHEDULER STOPPED** panel if nothing checks in
for 16 minutes, so a misconfigured cron announces itself rather than looking
like a quiet day.

## 6. Point the phone at the deployment

On the app's sign-in screen, change the server address from
`http://10.0.2.2:3000` to `https://<your-app>.vercel.app`, then sign in.

Then build a real APK so it stops depending on a USB cable:

```bash
cd mobile
flutter build apk --release
```

The file lands in `mobile/build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk`.
Install it and the laptop is out of the loop entirely.

---

## Why the region is pinned

`vercel.json` sets `"regions": ["cle1"]` — Cleveland, which is AWS
**us-east-2**, the same region as the Neon database.

This is the single biggest performance decision in the project. Measured from
a laptop in India against that database:

```
one warm query      ~296ms      <- almost entirely network distance
12 in parallel      ~600ms
```

A screen refresh makes roughly a dozen queries. In the same region those round
trips drop to single-digit milliseconds, so the same work costs ~30ms instead
of ~600ms. Deploying far from the database would throw that away and no amount
of query tuning would win it back.

If you ever move the Neon project to a different region, change this to match.
`node scripts/bench-db.mjs` prints the current latency picture.

## After deploying

- Watch the first tick land: the red scheduler panel should clear within 5 minutes.
- **"SCHEDULER NEVER STARTED" appears once on a fresh deployment** — the heartbeat
  row does not exist yet. The first tick clears it. Not a fault.
- `LINKEDIN_LIVE=true` means real posts on a real profile. Leave it `false` for
  a day if you want to watch the cadence before it goes live.

---

# Backups and restore

A GitHub Action (`.github/workflows/backup.yml`) dumps the database nightly at
19:40 UTC, encrypts it with AES-256, and keeps it as a build artifact for 90
days. It needs two repository secrets — `DATABASE_URL` and `BACKUP_PASSPHRASE`.

The parts worth protecting are the published archive, the writing samples and
the edit notes: the agent's learned voice. Everything else can be rebuilt from
this repository.

## Restoring

1. Open the repo on GitHub → **Actions** → **Backup** → pick a run → download
   the `db-backup-YYYY-MM-DD` artifact and unzip it.
2. Decrypt it with the passphrase you stored as `BACKUP_PASSPHRASE`:

   ```
   gpg --decrypt --output restored.dump backup-YYYY-MM-DD.dump.gpg
   ```

3. Inspect before you touch anything real:

   ```
   pg_restore --list restored.dump
   ```

4. Restore into a NEW empty database first, never over the live one:

   ```
   pg_restore --no-owner --no-privileges --dbname "$NEW_DATABASE_URL" restored.dump
   ```

Point `DATABASE_URL` at the restored database only once you have looked at it.

---

# Running the tests

```
npm test          # pure logic, no database, ~1s
npm run test:db   # every query against a real Postgres
npm run build:check
cd mobile && flutter analyze lib test && flutter test
```

`npm run test:db` needs a **throwaway** database — it creates and deletes
agents. Never point it at the live one. Locally:

```
createdb linkdin_dbtest
DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/linkdin_dbtest npm run test:db
```

CI runs all of these on every push to `main` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`),
using a disposable Postgres container for the database job.

**Why this suite exists separately from `npm test`:** `scripts/selftest.ts` is
pure logic and never opens a connection, so invalid SQL that is valid
TypeScript passes it. That is exactly how `listDueSlots` shipped with an
ambiguous column and the scheduler never ran once, with every test green.

---

# Keeping it alive

Five things can stop this app months from now. Four are handled; the fifth needs
you to know about it.

## 1. The LinkedIn token expires every 60 days — HANDLED

It cannot renew itself. The watchdog pushes a notification at 7 days remaining
and again once it has expired. Reconnect from the Status tab.

## 2. The cron stops — HANDLED

`schedulerHealth()` marks the scheduler stale after 16 minutes without a tick,
the Schedule tab shouts, and the watchdog pushes.

## 3. The database fills up — HANDLED

`lib/retention.ts` sweeps the tables that grow without bound, once a day, from
the cron tick. `rejections` is the one that mattered: twenty to forty rows per
cycle, several cycles a day, forever.

Kept deliberately: `posts` (the archive IS the product, and the writer reads it
for voice) and `distributions` (publish idempotency — deleting a row could let a
post send twice).

## 4. Backups — HANDLED

Nightly, encrypted, 90 days. See the restore steps above.

## 5. GitHub Actions minutes run out — HANDLED, but watch it

A **private** repo on the free plan gets **2,000 Actions minutes a month**, and
every job is rounded UP to a whole minute. Exhausting them does not degrade
gracefully: Actions stop entirely until the next billing cycle, which silently
takes the nightly backup and the watchdog with it — the two things that exist to
notice failure.

The watchdog was originally every 30 minutes. That is 48 runs a day of a
fifteen-second curl, each billed as a full minute: **1,440 minutes a month, 72%
of the allowance, spent watching**. It now runs every three hours — 240 minutes
a month, and still detects a dead scheduler within three hours.

The Flutter checks are split into their own workflow so they only run when
`mobile/**` changes. A backend commit does not pay for a Flutter toolchain, and
a documentation change pays for nothing at all.

Current budget, roughly:

| | minutes/month |
|---|---|
| Watchdog, every 3h | 240 |
| Backup, nightly | 30 |
| CI, an active month | ~150 |
| **Total** | **~420 of 2,000** |

Check it occasionally at **Settings → Billing → Plans and usage**. If it ever
climbs, the watchdog cadence is the dial to turn.

### A note if you ever make this repository public

Scheduled workflows are **automatically disabled after 60 days with no
repository activity — in public repositories only.** It does not apply while
this repo is private, which is why nothing here works around it. Going public
trades unlimited Actions minutes for that rule, and you would then need a commit
every 60 days or the schedules stop.

Either way, the `Health check` readout on the Status tab is how you would find
out: it shows how long since the watchdog last ran. Minutes is normal. Hours or
days means the workflows are off, whatever the cause.

## 6. Feeds die quietly — HANDLED

Every fetch records its outcome in `feed_health`. A feed that fails six times in
a row AND has not succeeded for three days is reported once a week. Both
conditions are needed: consecutive failures alone would fire during any host
outage, and "no success lately" alone would flag a feed nobody is fetching
because its category is switched off.

A 200 response that parses to zero items counts as a failure. `parseFeed` does
not filter by date, so even a dormant blog returns its old entries — zero really
does mean the format changed, or that it was not a feed at all, which is what a
redesigned site returns as an HTML error page with a 200 status.

## 7. LinkedIn retires the API version — HANDLED

`LINKEDIN_API_VERSION` is pinned (currently `202607`) and LinkedIn sunsets
versions about twelve months after release. At ten months old the watchdog
starts reminding you weekly, which leaves two months to act. The fix is bumping
that one variable in Vercel.

Without this the first sign would have been a post that failed to send — an
alert that arrives strictly after the damage.

## 8. Neon's compute allowance runs out — HANDLED BY A SETTING

Neon's free tier gives 100 CU-hours of compute a month. The smallest compute is
0.25 CU, so the allowance is 400 wall-clock hours of a *running* database —
against 730 hours in a month. A compute that never suspends therefore uses
**182 CU-hours**, and the database is dead for the last third of every month.

Two rules keep this comfortable:

**Pin the compute to 0.25 CU, min AND max.** Neon defaults new projects to
autoscaling `0.25 ↔ 2 CU`. This database is ~30 MB serving small indexed
queries and never needs more, but the ceiling is real: at 2 CU the same usage
bills eight times as fast and exhausts the month in about a week. Console →
Branches → `production` → the Primary compute → Edit → set both ends to
0.25 CU. Do the same under Settings → Default compute size so new branches
inherit it.

**Never add a keep-alive ping.** See the warning in the README's cron section.
Letting the database suspend is the whole reason the budget works.

With both in place the bill is just the tick waking it: a 15-minute cron
against Neon's 5-minute suspend delay is roughly 6 hours of compute a day,
about 48 CU-hours a month — comfortably inside the allowance with room for the
dashboard and the phone.

Watch it on the project dashboard: Compute, "since <date>". Halfway through the
cycle it should read under 50.

---

# Security

## What is protected

| | |
|---|---|
| Every `/api` route | fail-closed session gate in `middleware.ts`; a new route is protected by default |
| Login | HMAC session cookie, httpOnly + secure + sameSite; 8 failures per 15 min per client, counted in Postgres so concurrent instances cannot dodge it |
| LinkedIn token | AES-256-GCM at rest, key never in the database |
| Cron and watchdog | `X-Cron-Secret`, timing-safe compare, 404 on mismatch so they do not advertise that they exist |
| SQL | every statement parameterised; the only interpolated identifiers are literals in `lib/retention.ts` |
| Uploads | type allowlist (JPG/PNG/GIF) and a 4MB cap |
| Browser | HSTS, nosniff, frame-ancestors none, referrer policy, permissions policy |

## If you lose the phone, or think the password leaked

**Change `APP_SECRET` in Vercel and redeploy.** Every session everywhere dies
instantly, because the cookie is a signature over that secret and nothing else.
Change `APP_PASSWORD` too if the password itself is the worry.

This is the revocation mechanism. There is no "sign out everywhere" button:
sessions are verified in Edge middleware, which cannot reach Postgres, so
there is nowhere to keep a revocation list. Rotating the secret does the same
job in about thirty seconds.

## Known and accepted

- **One password, no second factor.** Proportionate for one user behind a URL
  nobody has. If this ever gets a second user, it needs real accounts.
- **Sessions last 30 days.** A stolen unlocked phone is a real session until you
  rotate `APP_SECRET`.
- **`google-services.json` is committed.** Not a credential — Firebase documents
  it as public, it ships inside every APK, and the key is scoped to the package.
  The service-account key is NOT in the repository.

````

## Source: DESIGN.md

````text
# ByLine design system

The Android and Windows app now follows the light, responsive design documented in
[the ByLine UX redesign plan](reports/ByLine-UX-redesign-plan.md), with live tokens
in `mobile/lib/theme.dart`. That plan supersedes the dark palette, typography and
layout directions below for the native app. The following is retained as the
historical design reference for the existing web interface.

## Historical reference: Ink & Filament

The source of truth for how this product looks and behaves. Every value in
`mobile/lib/theme.dart` and `app/globals.css` comes from here; nothing is
invented at a call site.

---

## 1. What this product actually is

Not a scheduler. Not a dashboard. **A one-person newsroom where the reporter
never sleeps and you hold the presses.**

An agent reads the wire overnight, judges what it finds against your standards,
and sets one story in your voice. Then it stops and waits for an editor. You
are that editor. The whole product is the moment between *copy exists* and
*copy goes out* — and that moment has a deadline.

That framing decides everything below. The vocabulary is a copy desk's, because
the app already thinks in those terms and did before this redesign: the **fold**
(what LinkedIn cuts at 210 characters), the **slot** (which in a real newsroom
is the copy chief's chair), **passed over**. Where a name was invented, it now
comes from the same world — as long as it stays readable; see §8.

What it is *not*: paper. No cream ground, no serif display, no fake newsprint.
The register is a dark instrument used at 07:00 with one hand. The newsroom
shows up in the information model and the language, never as pastiche.

### The daily loop, which the design must make fast

1. A notification, or you open the app.
2. **Is anything waiting on me, and how long have I got?**
3. Read the draft — properly, above the fold first.
4. Decide: let it go at its time / send it now / fix it / discard it.
5. Close the app.

Steps 2–4 are the product. Everything else is configuration you touch once.

---

## 2. Colour

A warm ink ground, because a blue-black ground is the default every dark app
reaches for and it makes the accents look like status LEDs. Warm ink reads as a
room with a lamp in it.

Colour encodes exactly one question: **which clock is this on?** Three accents,
each with a role. Nothing is coloured for decoration; a colour with no meaning
is a colour that teaches people to stop reading colour.

### Ground — ink

| Token | Hex | Job |
|---|---|---|
| `ink` | `#0E0D0B` | The page. Copy sits directly on it. |
| `ink2` | `#161512` | Raised: sheets, sticky bars, the object you act on. |
| `ink3` | `#1E1C18` | Wells: inputs, pressed states, meter tracks. |
| `rule` | `#2A2721` | Hairline. Separation without a box. |
| `ruleStrong` | `#3B372F` | A real edge — inputs, outlined buttons. |

### Ink on the page — paper

| Token | Hex | Contrast on `ink` | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| `paper` | `#F2EFE9` | 16.9:1 | Copy. The post itself, headings. |
| `paperDim` | `#B3ADA2` | 8.7:1 | Secondary prose, descriptions. |
| `paperFaint` | `#8A857B` | 5.3:1 | Captions, slugs, disabled. |

`paperFaint` is deliberately lighter than the value it replaces (`#6A7383`,
3.9:1), which failed WCAG AA at the 12px sizes it was used at.

### The three accents

| Token | Hex | Contrast | Means |
|---|---|---|---|
| `filament` | `#E8A76B` | 9.4:1 | **On the desk.** Still yours. Drafts, countdowns, the fold, review windows, anything you can still change your mind about. |
| `daylight` | `#7FB3C4` | 8.5:1 | **Out in the world.** Published, cleared, connected, healthy. Settled and cold. |
| `flare` | `#D9736E` | 6.1:1 | **Broken.** Missed, failed, expired, disconnected. Needs a human. |

These are **desaturated on purpose**, and that was a correction. The first cut
used `#FF8A3D`, `#45C8DC` and `#FF4D5E` — fully saturated, and against a
near-black ground they read as status LEDs rather than as ink. On a screen you
open at 07:00 to read one careful paragraph, that is the wrong temperature: it
makes an ordinary morning look like an incident.

Pulling each hue back toward paper cost nothing in legibility — every value
still clears AA comfortably, because contrast comes from lightness and the
saturation was never doing that work.

A fourth state — a slot that read its candidates and chose silence — gets
**no colour at all**, only `paperFaint`. Correct behaviour must never look like
an alarm; that is how you teach someone to distrust a quiet day.

The previous system carried five accents (`draft`, `live`, `alarm`, `good`,
`attention`). `good` and `live` always meant the same thing to a reader —
*settled, nothing to do* — so they are one colour now. Chanel's rule: take one
thing off.

Washes for fills are precomputed solids rather than alpha, so a fill never
shifts when it lands on a different ground: `filamentWash #2A1B0F`,
`daylightWash #0E2A30`, `flareWash #2C1214`.

`filament` has a second job, and the two never co-occur: in CONTENT it means
"on the desk", and in a CONTROL it means "selected". A chip and a draft are
never the same object, so no ambiguity arises — and a settings screen where
nothing is ever accented is one where the selected state is hard to find.

Colour also marks the **abnormal case only**. `running`, `live` and `waits for
you` are the ordinary state of a healthy agent; lighting all three lit three
colours on an ordinary day, which is three colours saying nothing. `paused`,
`dry run` and `publishes itself` are the three that make someone say "wait,
what?" — those carry the accent, their opposites stay quiet.

**Colour is never the only signal.** Every state carries an icon and a word.

---

## 3. Type

Three faces, three jobs, no overlap.

| Face | Role | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Barlow Condensed** 500/600/700 | *The slug* | Section rules, screen titles, masthead, status chips, day initials. Uppercase, tracked out. Condensed because a phone column is narrow and a newsroom deck always was. |
| **IBM Plex Sans** (variable) | *The copy* | The post. Descriptions, buttons, anything read as language. |
| **IBM Plex Mono** 400/600/700 | *The clock* | Times, counts, scores, ids, countdowns. Tabular figures always. |

Barlow Condensed ships **static** instances, which matters: a variable axis in a
`TextStyle` silently makes it non-const and breaks const widget trees (logged in
`~/dev/design-references/PATTERNS.md`). Statics keep every style const.

The post is set in Plex Sans and not in something more characteristic on
purpose. This screen's job is to predict what a reader sees in the LinkedIn
feed; setting it in a display face would flatter copy that will not be rendered
that way. The character goes into the furniture around the copy, never into the
copy.

### Scale

| Token | Size / line | Face | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| `copy` | 17 / 1.62 | Sans 400 | **The post.** The most readable thing on screen, because reading it carefully *is* the job. |
| `body` | 15 / 1.5 | Sans 400 | Prose. |
| `small` | 13.5 / 1.45 | Sans 400 | Secondary prose. |
| `micro` | 12 / 1.4 | Sans 400 | Captions. |
| `slug` | 11.5, +1.4 tracking | Cond 600 | Eyebrows, chips, labels. Uppercase. |
| `rule` | 13, +1.2 tracking | Cond 600 | Section headings. Uppercase. |
| `title` | 22 | Cond 700 | Screen titles. |
| `display` | 34 | Cond 700 | Masthead. |
| `data` | 14 | Mono 600 tab | Any figure in a column. |
| `clock` | 44 | Mono 700 tab | The countdown. One per screen, at most. |

Tabular figures on anything that changes in place. A countdown whose digits
change width reflows while you read it, and a number that jitters reads as
broken.

---

## 4. Space, shape, motion

- **Rhythm** 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24 / 32 / 48. Nothing between.
- **Radius** 7 (chips, inputs) · 12 (objects) · 18 (sheets). Raised from 4/8/14:
  the tighter set read as an instrument, which was the intent, but combined
  with a visible border on every surface it also read as *tight*.
- **A card is a FILL, not an outline.** Separation comes from the raised ground
  and the space around it. Drawing a border on top of a fill states the same
  thing twice, and a page of outlined rectangles is what reads as cramped no
  matter how much padding sits inside them. Only the one object with a deadline
  gets an edge you actually notice.
- **Touch** 48px minimum, 8px minimum between adjacent targets.
- **Motion** one duration — 180ms, ease-out — for every state change. 320ms for
  route transitions. Reduced motion is honoured by not building the timeline,
  not by shortening it.

The single orchestrated moment: when an uncleared draft crosses into its last
two minutes, the clock moves `filament → flare` and the card's edge brightens
once. That is the only animation in the app that is not a state change, and it
earns its place because it marks the last point at which a decision is still
possible.

---

## 5. The signature: the fold

LinkedIn cuts a post at 210 characters and hides the rest behind *see more*.
That cut happens on a phone, which makes a phone the right place to judge
whether the hook survives it. Drawing the boundary is the single most useful
thing this app does that LinkedIn's own composer does not.

So it is drawn properly: a dashed cut in `filament` straight across the copy
column, breaking for a mono counter in the gutter —

```
╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌  FOLD · 340 BELOW  ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
```

— and the rule *is* the control. Copy starts collapsed, because what you see
first must be exactly what a reader scrolling their feed sees first.

Everything else stays quiet. One memorable element, executed precisely.

---

## 6. Layout: the card is not the default

The previous design put every screen inside a stack of identical bordered
panels, so nothing had hierarchy and the post — the one thing on screen worth
reading — was about a third of the box it sat in, competing with badges, five
score meters, a rationale and four unlabelled icon buttons.

The rule now:

> **Copy sits on the page. A box means an object you act on.**

Sections are separated by rhythm and a hairline with a Condensed slug on it.
A bordered surface appears for exactly three things: a draft awaiting a
decision, a posting slot, and a sheet. Anything else — settings, readouts,
history, diagnostics — is a list on the ground.

---

## 7. Information architecture

Five bottom-bar destinations, three of which were "set once and revisit",
became **three**, plus writing as a task rather than a place.

| Destination | Holds | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Desk** | The deadline, drafts waiting on you, today's rail, anything broken | The daily loop, on one screen. The countdown used to live one tab away from the list of things it applied to. |
| **Archive** | Published · Passed over | Retrospective and read-only. Separated from Desk because nothing here needs a decision. |
| **Settings** | Timetable · Voice · Topics · LinkedIn · Diagnostics | Five configuration surfaces behind one index, each with a live one-line summary so the index answers most questions without being opened. |

**Compose is a full-screen route, not a tab.** Writing has a beginning and an
end; a tab makes it ambient and keeps stale state alive forever. Editing a
draft pushes the same route with the post loaded, which also removes the
cross-tab "bring the composer forward" hack the old shell needed. Leaving with
typed text asks first.

**There is no floating action button.** Every draft on the Desk ends in its own
row of buttons, and a control floating in the bottom-right corner sits
permanently on top of them — it covered "Send now" on the one card with a
deadline. It was also a claim this app cannot support: the recurring job is
DECIDING on what the agent wrote, not writing your own, and a FAB announces
itself as the main action on the screen. Write sits in each screen's header
instead.

### The draft card, top to bottom

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ p-0142 · AGENT · MUSIC-TECH       4h ago │  slug line
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ⚡ Sends at 09:30, in 2h 14m              │  the clock strip
│                                          │
│  Copy, set at 17/1.62 directly on the    │
│  ground. No inner box.                   │
│ ╌╌╌╌╌  FOLD · 340 BELOW  ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌ │  the signature
│                                          │
│  #MusicTech                              │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ Why this one                    8.4/10 │  collapsed: rationale + scores
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ Clear for 09:30 ]  [ Send now ]    ⋯   │  named actions, never mystery icons
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Judge scores and editorial reasoning collapse behind one disclosure carrying
the total. They are the answer to *why did it pick this*, which is a question
asked occasionally — not five progress bars competing with the copy every time.

Actions are labelled. The old card offered send-now, edit and discard as three
unlabelled 48px icon squares, which is the least legible way to present three
irreversible-ish choices. Swipe is added as an accelerator — right to clear,
left to discard, both reversible — but never as the only path to an action.

---

## 8. Words

Named by what the editor controls, never by how the system is built. Active
voice. An action keeps its name through the whole flow: the button that says
*Discard* produces *Discarded*.

| Say | Not |
|---|---|
| Clear | Approve |
| Send now | Publish immediately |
| Passed over | Rejected |
| Stayed quiet | No post generated |
| On the desk | Pending review |
| The scheduler stopped | Cron error |

Where the newsroom metaphor and plain language disagreed, plain language won.
An earlier draft of this used **spike** for discarding copy — a real term, and
the right one for a desk — but one the reader has to learn. The framing earns
its place in the *structure* (the Desk, the fold, the day's rail, what a
posting time is), never by making a verb harder to read.

"Clear" lost its time, too. `Clear for 09:30` said the time twice — it is
already in the countdown caption directly above — and at 390pt it wrapped the
most-pressed button in the app onto two lines.

Empty screens are an invitation, not a shrug: *"Nothing on the desk. The agent
reads on its timetable and stays quiet on days when nothing clears the bar —
check the Archive to see what it passed over."*

Errors say what happened and what to do, in the interface's voice. They do not
apologise and they are never vague.

---

## 9. Quality floor

- Touch targets 48px; 8px between them.
- Every colour pairing above 4.5:1 on its own ground; every state also carries
  an icon and a word.
- Reduced motion genuinely honoured.
- No layout shift from a countdown — tabular figures, reserved width.
- Verified by screenshot on a real handset at 1080×2400, not an emulator, and
  not by assuming it compiled.

````

## Source: README.md

````text
# ByLine

**Start here:** [Complete project handbook (PDF)](output/pdf/ByLine-Complete-Project-Handbook.pdf)
| [Download Android APK](https://github.com/Don-Gabriel/link_agent/raw/refs/heads/main/releases/android/byline-latest.apk)
| [Phone installation guide](releases/android/README.md)
| [Documentation and every-file reference](docs/README.md)

The downloadable Android release uses the dedicated [Cloudflare backend](cloud/README.md)
and works without the development computer. The original Next.js/PostgreSQL web
deployment described below remains a separate runtime. See the
[current verification report](reports/ByLine-release-verification-2026-11-07.md)
and [APK metadata/checksum](releases/android/release.json) for this repository snapshot.

A writing workspace for LinkedIn: discover relevant stories, prepare posts in
your voice, and review them before publishing. Choose from **1,112 subjects**
across 55 specialist groups, combine industries, and add your own editorial focus.

The native app includes account setup, optional voice preferences, writing samples,
a timetable, a composer, and a post archive. Setup and regular drafts use the same
writer and voice rules. See [local development](BYLINE-LOCAL.md) and
[live operation](BYLINE-LIVE.md) for the native app; the operator setup below
documents the original web deployment.

Forked from the autonomous-creator pipeline (discover → judge → write, behind a
Postgres advisory lock) and retargeted at a real professional profile. The
important change is that a cycle produces a **draft**, and publishing is a
separate, guarded decision.

## What it does

- **At your chosen posting times**, it pulls fresh candidates across
  your categories, scores every one in a single batched LLM call on five
  criteria, and writes a post about the winner — **only if it clears 6.5/10**.
  A story must also score at least 7/10 for subject fit and 6/10 for author fit.
  If no relevant source qualifies, it waits rather than forcing an unrelated post.
- **Approval queue by default.** Drafts wait for you with their scores, the
  editorial reasoning, and a marker showing exactly where LinkedIn will cut the
  text off. Flip auto-publish on once the voice sounds like you.
- **Your own posts**, with images, an optional pass to tighten the hook, and
  publish-now or save-as-draft.
- **Optional voice setup**: 10 tones, free-form instructions, writing samples,
  audience, structure, word range, openings, closings, emoji, hashtags and phrases
  to avoid. Skip customization to start with a professional voice, then edit it later.
- **Searchable subjects**: select up to 12 at once, including specialist areas
  across industries. Specialist sources use targeted news searches and must pass
  editorial relevance checks. Source availability varies by subject and date.
- **Optional signatures**, disabled for new native accounts. Existing accounts
  retain their saved preferences.

## Verification

```sh
npm test
npm run test:catalogue
npm run build:check
cd mobile
flutter analyze
flutter test
```

With the isolated local database and backend running, `npm run test:catalogue:api`
checks setup and persistence without model calls or LinkedIn publishing.

## Setup

### 1. Create the LinkedIn app

At [linkedin.com/developers/apps](https://www.linkedin.com/developers/apps):

1. **Create app.** It must be associated with a LinkedIn Page — a throwaway
   page is fine, it is only for app ownership and is not what you post to.
2. **Products tab** → request both:
   - *Sign In with LinkedIn using OpenID Connect* — identity, gives the person URN
   - *Share on LinkedIn* — gives `w_member_social`, the permission to post

   Both are self-serve and approve in minutes. You do **not** need the
   Community Management API; that one is a real review process and is only
   required for posting to company Pages.
3. **Auth tab** → add redirect URLs. Add both:
   - `http://localhost:3000/api/linkedin/callback`
   - `https://<your-app>.vercel.app/api/linkedin/callback`

   These must match `LINKEDIN_REDIRECT_URI` byte for byte. A trailing slash
   mismatch is the single most common cause of a failed connection.
4. Copy the Client ID and Client Secret.

### 2. Configure

```bash
cp .env.example .env
npm run keygen    # prints TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, APP_SECRET and CRON_SECRET
```

Fill in `DATABASE_URL` (Neon), `GEMINI_API_KEY`, the two LinkedIn values, and
the generated secrets. Set `APP_PASSWORD` to something only you know — that
password is the only thing between the internet and your profile.

Leave `LINKEDIN_LIVE=false` for now.

### 3. Run

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open <http://localhost:3000>, sign in with `APP_PASSWORD`, and complete setup:
your name, what you write about, categories, timezone and daily post time. The
schema applies itself on first database access.

Then **Connect LinkedIn** in the sidebar and approve the consent screen.

### 4. Watch it before you trust it

Leave `LINKEDIN_LIVE=false` for the first few days. The agent drafts on
schedule and the queue fills up, but nothing can reach LinkedIn — the publish
path refuses at the first check. Read the drafts. When they sound like you,
set `LINKEDIN_LIVE=true` and publish one by hand. Only after that is
auto-publish worth turning on.

### 5. Schedule the cron

The agent only acts when something pings its tick endpoint. Every 15 minutes:

```bash
curl -H "X-Cron-Secret: $CRON_SECRET" https://<your-app>.vercel.app/api/cron/tick
```

Use [cron-job.org](https://cron-job.org) or a GitHub Actions schedule. Two
overlapping triggers are harmless — every cycle passes through the same
advisory lock, and every publish through its own idempotency key.

**Do not add a keep-alive ping.** An earlier version of this file suggested
hitting `/api/health` every few minutes to stop Neon's free tier autosuspending
after ~5 idle minutes. Do not: that endpoint runs a query, so pinging it holds
the compute open around the clock. At Neon's smallest compute that is
0.25 CU × 730 h = **182 CU-hours a month against a 100 CU-hour allowance** —
the database is suspended for the last third of every month, and the agent
stops posting. It buys about a second of cold start and costs the whole budget.

Let it suspend. The tick wakes it, and `connectionTimeoutMillis` in
[lib/db.ts](lib/db.ts) is already set to 20s precisely so the first request
after a quiet spell waits for the wake-up instead of failing.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # local development
npm run build        # type-check and production build
npm test             # self-test: text escaping, length accounting, scheduler
npm run check:feeds  # which RSS sources are actually reachable from your network
npm run keygen       # generate the three secrets
```

## Things that will bite you

1. **Tokens last 60 days and cannot renew themselves.** LinkedIn issues
   programmatic refresh tokens only to approved Marketing Developer Platform
   partners; a standard self-serve app gets 60 days and nothing else. The
   dashboard warns from day 50 and pauses cleanly at expiry. Reconnecting is
   one click and loses nothing. This is the one unavoidable manual step, and
   anyone promising otherwise is either an approved partner or scraping.

2. **Never automate linkedin.com with a browser.** Playwright against the real
   site violates the terms and gets accounts restricted. Everything here goes
   through the official API.

3. **Ambiguous sends are not retried.** If LinkedIn never answers, we cannot
   tell whether the post went out — reading your own posts back needs
   `r_member_social`, a restricted scope this app does not have. So the send is
   frozen, flagged in the dashboard, and you are asked to check your profile
   and say what happened. Retrying automatically is how you end up posting
   twice to a real audience.

4. **Fifteen characters must be escaped in post text.** LinkedIn's "little"
   format reserves `\ | { } @ [ ] ( ) < > # * _ ~`, and an unescaped
   parenthesis in ordinary prose is enough to corrupt a post. This is handled
   in one place (`lib/linkedin.ts`) and covered by `npm test` — do not build a
   second path to the Posts API that skips it.

5. **The 3000-character limit applies to the escaped text.** Prose full of
   parentheses can gain a hundred-plus characters when escaped, so a post that
   looks fine can be rejected. `checkLength` measures the escaped form.

6. **Some feed URLs are unverified.** Several music-tech hosts were unreachable
   from the network this was built on, which may mean the feed is dead or may
   mean that network blocked them. They are marked `verified: false` in
   `lib/discovery.ts`. Run `npm run check:feeds` from your own machine to find
   out; a dead feed costs one logged warning per cycle and nothing else.

## File map

```
lib/linkedin.ts     LinkedIn API client — little-text escaping, posts, images, OAuth
lib/distribute.ts   the publish path: idempotency claim, definite vs ambiguous failure
lib/accounts.ts     token storage, the 60-day expiry policy
lib/crypto.ts       AES-256-GCM for tokens at rest
lib/auth.ts         dashboard session, enforced by middleware.ts
lib/cycle.ts        the daily orchestrator, behind the advisory lock
lib/discovery.ts    category-grouped feeds, interleaved so one feed can't dominate
lib/judge.ts        batched scoring, 5 criteria, category assignment
lib/writer.ts       LinkedIn voice, the rationed Marvel line, custom-post polish
lib/format.ts       deterministic assembly: source line, hashtags, length checks
lib/schedule.ts     daily cadence in your timezone
lib/categories.ts   the three categories and their hashtag vocabulary
app/page.tsx        gate, setup, dashboard
```

## Deploying

Push to a repo, import it in Vercel, and set every variable from `.env` in the
project settings — including `LINKEDIN_REDIRECT_URI` pointing at the deployed
domain, and that same URL registered on the LinkedIn app. Then point the cron
at the deployed `/api/cron/tick`.

````

## Source: app/api/account/delete/route.ts

````text
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import { requestIdentity } from '../../../../lib/request-agent';
import { getPool } from '../../../../lib/db';
export const dynamic='force-dynamic';

/** User-scoped removal. No provider calls and no deletion of LinkedIn posts. */
export async function POST(request:Request) {
  const user=await requestIdentity();
  if(!user)return NextResponse.json({error:'Sign in to delete your ByLine account.'},{status:401});
  const body=await request.json().catch(()=>null);
  if(body?.confirmation!=='DELETE')return NextResponse.json({error:'Type DELETE to confirm account deletion.'},{status:400});
  const c=await getPool()!.connect();
  try {
    await c.query('BEGIN');
    await c.query("SET LOCAL lock_timeout='5s'");
    // Parent row locks also serialize new child inserts and publish claims.
    await c.query('SELECT id FROM byline_users WHERE id=$1 FOR UPDATE',[user.userId]);
    const agents=await c.query('SELECT id FROM agents WHERE owner_id=$1 FOR UPDATE',[user.userId]);
    const ids=agents.rows.map(a=>a.id);
    for(const id of ids) {
      const lock=await c.query('SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(42,hashtext($1)) AS locked',[id]);
      if(!lock.rows[0].locked)throw new Error('busy');
      const slots=await c.query('SELECT id FROM post_slots WHERE agent_id=$1',[id]);
      for(const slot of slots.rows) {
        const lock=await c.query('SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(43,hashtext($1)) AS locked',[slot.id]);
        if(!lock.rows[0].locked)throw new Error('busy');
      }
    }
    const sending=await c.query("SELECT 1 FROM distributions WHERE agent_id=ANY($1::uuid[]) AND status='in_flight' LIMIT 1",[ids]);
    if(sending.rowCount)throw new Error('publishing');
    // Fixed, reviewed identifiers: never accept table names from the request.
    for(const table of ['notification_outbox','review_deliveries','device_tokens','push_log','oauth_states',
      'linkedin_accounts','distributions','media_assets','rejections','scheduler_state','post_counters','posts','post_slots']) {
      await c.query(`DELETE FROM ${table} WHERE agent_id=ANY($1::uuid[])`,[ids]);
    }
    await c.query('DELETE FROM ai_usage WHERE owner=$1 OR owner=ANY($2::text[])',[user.userId,ids]);
    await c.query('DELETE FROM ai_user_days WHERE owner=$1 OR owner=ANY($2::text[])',[user.userId,ids]);
    for(const table of ['byline_sessions','native_auth','onboarding'])await c.query(`DELETE FROM ${table} WHERE user_id=$1`,[user.userId]);
    await c.query('DELETE FROM agents WHERE owner_id=$1',[user.userId]);
    await c.query('DELETE FROM byline_users WHERE id=$1',[user.userId]);
    await c.query('COMMIT');
    return NextResponse.json({ok:true,deleted:true});
  } catch(e) {
    await c.query('ROLLBACK');
    const reason=(e as Error).message;
    return NextResponse.json({error:reason==='publishing'
      ? 'A publish request is still unresolved. Check its outcome in My posts before deleting your account.'
      : 'Your account could not be deleted yet. Wait for any active preparation or upload to finish, then try again. No data was removed.'},{status:409});
  } finally {c.release();}
}

````

## Source: app/api/auth/route.ts

````text
import { requestIdentity } from '../../../lib/request-agent';
import { query } from '../../../lib/db';
/**
 * Login. POST a password, receive an httpOnly session cookie.
 *
 * Guessing is bounded two ways. The 800ms delay on failure slows a sequential
 * attacker, and lib/ratelimit.ts counts failures per client in Postgres so a
 * PARALLEL one is stopped too — twenty simultaneous guesses all wait the same
 * 800ms once, which on its own costs an attacker almost nothing. Behind this
 * gate is an endpoint that publishes to a real profile.
 */
import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { authConfigured, createSession, passwordMatches, SESSION_COOKIE } from "../../../lib/auth";
import {
  checkLoginAllowed,
  clearLoginFailures,
  clientKey,
  MAX_ATTEMPTS,
  recordLoginFailure,
} from "../../../lib/ratelimit";

export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  if (!authConfigured()) {
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: "auth_not_configured", detail: "Set APP_PASSWORD and APP_SECRET." },
      { status: 503 },
    );
  }

  const client = clientKey(request);
  const verdict = await checkLoginAllowed(client);
  if (!verdict.allowed) {
    // Checked BEFORE reading the body and before comparing anything, so a
    // blocked client cannot learn whether a password was close by timing.
    return NextResponse.json(
      {
        error: "too_many_attempts",
        detail: `${MAX_ATTEMPTS} failed attempts. Try again in ${verdict.retryAfterMinutes} minute${verdict.retryAfterMinutes === 1 ? "" : "s"}.`,
      },
      { status: 429, headers: { "Retry-After": String(verdict.retryAfterMinutes * 60) } },
    );
  }

  let password = "";
  try {
    password = ((await request.json()) as { password?: string }).password ?? "";
  } catch {
    return NextResponse.json({ error: "bad_request" }, { status: 400 });
  }

  if (!(await passwordMatches(password))) {
    await recordLoginFailure(client);
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 800));
    return NextResponse.json({ error: "invalid_password" }, { status: 401 });
  }

  // A correct password forgives this client's history, so a few fat-fingered
  // attempts never accumulate into a lockout during ordinary use.
  await clearLoginFailures(client);
  const session = await createSession();
  const response = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
  response.cookies.set(SESSION_COOKIE, session.value, {
    httpOnly: true,
    sameSite: "lax",
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
    path: "/",
    maxAge: session.maxAge,
  });
  return response;
}

/** Logout. */
export async function DELETE() {
  const identity = await requestIdentity();
  if (identity) await query('UPDATE byline_sessions SET revoked_at=now() WHERE id=$1', [identity.sessionId]);
  const response = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
  response.cookies.set(SESSION_COOKIE, "", { path: "/", maxAge: 0 });
  return response;
}

````

## Source: app/api/compose/rewrite/route.ts

````text
/**
 * Rewrite arbitrary composer text — no saved post required.
 *
 * The sibling action on /api/posts/[seq] rewrites a draft that already exists
 * in the database. That is useless while someone is still typing something new,
 * which is exactly when a second opinion is most wanted. So this takes the text
 * directly and saves nothing: the composer shows the variant beside what the
 * author wrote and they decide.
 *
 * One LLM call, button-triggered. `variant` cycles the angle the writer is told
 * to take, so pressing it repeatedly gives genuinely different options rather
 * than the same sentence reshuffled.
 */
import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { getPersona, voiceReferencesFor } from "../../../../lib/agents";
import { getRequestAgent } from "../../../../lib/request-agent";
import { MAX_BODY_CHARS } from "../../../../lib/format";
import { rewriteDraft } from "../../../../lib/writer";

export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";
// Same reason as /api/posts/[seq]: the rewrite may be followed by a repair call.
export const maxDuration = 120;

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const agent = await getRequestAgent();
  if (!agent) return NextResponse.json({ error: "not_initialized" }, { status: 400 });

  // Fetched together: two independent reads against a database that is not in
  // the same country, and awaiting them in sequence adds a round trip to every
  // press of a button the user is already waiting on an LLM for.
  const [persona, voice] = await Promise.all([
    getPersona(agent.agentId),
    voiceReferencesFor(agent),
  ]);
  if (!persona) return NextResponse.json({ error: "persona_not_ready" }, { status: 409 });

  let body: { text?: string; variant?: number };
  try {
    body = (await request.json()) as typeof body;
  } catch {
    return NextResponse.json({ error: "bad_request" }, { status: 400 });
  }

  const text = (body.text ?? "").trim();
  if (text.length < 20) {
    return NextResponse.json({ error: "text_too_short" }, { status: 400 });
  }
  if (text.length > MAX_BODY_CHARS) {
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: "text_too_long", detail: `${text.length} chars, max ${MAX_BODY_CHARS}` },
      { status: 400 },
    );
  }

  const variant = await rewriteDraft(persona, text, agent.style, Number(body.variant ?? 0), voice);
  if (!variant.ok) {
    return NextResponse.json({ error: "rewrite_failed", detail: variant.reason }, { status: 502 });
  }

  // Preview the rewritten body and tags together under the current voice cap.
  // Neither replaces the composer's contents until the user accepts it.
  return NextResponse.json({
    ok: true,
    text: variant.data.text,
    hashtags: (variant.data.hashtags ?? []).slice(0, agent.style.hashtagCount),
    servedBy: variant.data.servedBy,
  });
}
````
